name: Silent Cam
specific_features: Automated beacon (distress, navigation, or unknown purpose)
description: Silent Cam is a tiny, tidally locked barren body orbiting close to its parent planet, its surface an unremarkable expanse of cratered gray rock distinguished only by a series of cam-shaped lobes along its equator. These geological formations, smoothly curved asymmetric ridges, give the moon a slightly irregular profile that is visible from its parent world. The sunlit hemisphere is heat-blasted and featureless, while the dark side is cratered and frozen, the terminator line a jagged boundary between the two extremes.

The absolute silence and near-zero gravity of Silent Cam create an environment that feels less like a place and more like an absence of place. The surface offers no landmark, no variation, no point of interest beyond the cam-shaped ridges that give the body its name. Standing on the dark side, the parent planet fills a significant portion of the sky, its light reflecting off the gray regolith with a cold, indirect glow. On the bright side, the unfiltered sunlight is blinding against the pale rock.

A single automated beacon sits on the highest point of the largest cam ridge, broadcasting a navigation signal of standard format but unknown origin. The beacon predates any recorded settlement in the system and runs on a power source that has not been identified despite physical examination. Its signal includes data packets that appear to be sensor readings from the beacon's immediate vicinity, continuously monitoring seismic activity, radiation levels, and the gravitational relationship between Silent Cam and its parent planet.

Silent Cam has no strategic or economic value, yet the beacon continues its tireless monitoring, suggesting someone or something considers the tiny moon worth watching. Analysis of the beacon's accumulated data reveals subtle changes in Silent Cam's orbital parameters that would be undetectable by any other means, a gradual shift in the moon's orientation relative to its parent planet. The cam-shaped ridges appear to be oriented in a pattern that will, over millennia, cause the tidal locking to release, allowing the moon to begin rotating. Whether this is a natural process or one the beacon was placed to observe, and perhaps to trigger, remains an open question.
